column3: Explicitly commands humanity not to worship Satan, making it the closest verbal and thematic parallel.
A declaration of faith does not clarify Satanic worship, rebellion, or Ibrahim's warning.
God's mercy provides a broad backdrop to the divine name in the focus ayah, without addressing Satan or worship.
The next verse continues Ibrahim's address to his father, warning that he may become Satan's ally through punishment from the Most Merciful.
The Merciful Lord's greeting of peace only generally resonates with the divine name in the focus ayah.
The repeated names of the Most Merciful and Merciful illuminate the divine name against which Satan is described as rebellious.
Identifies Satan as humanity's clear enemy and as a source of discord, supporting Ibrahim's warning against serving him.
The father's hostile reply is the immediate narrative consequence of Ibrahim's warning against his worship.
Ibrahim says idols have led many astray and contrasts following him with disobeying him, closely extending the focus warning.
Uses the title the Most Merciful within a dispute over proper worship, though its immediate argument differs.
Solomon's horses do not clarify Satanic worship or rebellion toward the Most Merciful.
A promise not to disobey a teacher is only a general contrast to Satan's rebellion.
Names Satan's allies and contrasts their cause with God's, supporting the focus ayah's warning about allegiance.
God's mercy granted to Ibrahim follows the conflict with his father, continuing the local narrative at a distance.
Noah's command to worship God alone and warning of punishment closely parallels the prophetic corrective form of the focus ayah.
The attribution of a child to the Most Merciful concerns the same divine name but not Satanic worship.
Satanic labor under Solomon does not bear on worshiping Satan or his rebellion.
Satanic incitement of disbelievers helps explain the corrupting influence Ibrahim warns his father to reject.
Ibrahim's preceding question exposes his father's idols as powerless, directly grounding the warning not to serve Satan.
Submission to Solomon does not clarify worship of Satan or the Most Merciful.
Jacob warns his son of Satan's clear enmity, reinforcing the focus ayah's portrayal of Satan as a danger.
A denial that the Most Merciful takes a child uses the same divine name but does not explain the warning.
Ibrahim's peaceful response and promise of prayer show the filial concern that governs his preceding warning.
Rejects powerless gods besides the Most Merciful, supporting the monotheistic alternative to serving Satan.
Previous worship obstructs the queen from guidance, a close parallel to Ibrahim's concern about his father's idolatry.
Idris's exaltation does not clarify the focus ayah.
Links denial with disobedience, providing a general counterpart to Satan's rebelliousness.
The Most Merciful's true kingship on Judgment Day is too general to explain Satanic service.
The elevation of the Prophet's remembrance is unrelated to the focus warning.
Disobeying a leader by failing to follow him is a distant formal parallel to rebellion.
John's goodness to his parents and lack of rebellion contrast with the father's rejection and Satan's rebelliousness.
Destruction of stronger towns does not clarify the focus ayah.
Disobeying God and His messenger has consequences, but the verse lacks the focus's Satanic-worship relation.
Joseph attributes family estrangement to Satan, offering a distant family-context parallel.
Commands knowledge of God's oneness, the essential theological alternative to serving Satan through idolatry.
Withdrawal from people and what they worship besides God, followed by mercy, closely parallels rejecting wrongful worship.
Following the caller before the Most Merciful is a distant obedience contrast, not a warning about Satan.
A community's threat to stone messengers resembles the father's later threat but does not clarify the focus itself.
Commands God's servants to worship Him alone, directly supplying the positive alternative to serving Satan.
Rejects inherited worship as following a call ultimately leading from Satan, directly illuminating Ibrahim's appeal to his father.
Calls Satan rebellious, directly echoing the focus description, though in a different setting.
Joins worshipers with what they worship, helping frame the relational nature of the father's idolatry.
A daughter's advice to her father about hiring does not clarify the focus ayah.
Passing by ruined towns offers no relevant connection.
Fear of disobeying the Lord provides a direct ethical contrast to Satan's rebellion toward the Most Merciful.
Unbelief in God is too general without a link to Satan, worship, or Ibrahim's address.
Job's suffering attributed to Satan is only a general Satan reference with a different function.
States that jinn and humans were created to worship God, directly contrasting proper worship with serving Satan.
Pharaoh's prior rebellion shows the seriousness of persistent disobedience, though without the focus's worship relation.
A description of Paradise wine is unrelated.
Marriage prohibitions and God's mercy do not clarify the focus ayah.
A son respectfully tells his father to obey God's command, a meaningful filial-obedience contrast.
Submission on Judgment Day does not add a specific connection.
Seeking forgiveness from the Merciful God is only an attribute-level parallel.
A prophet refuses to disobey God after receiving proof and mercy, paralleling the focus's opposition to rebellion.
The greeting to Noah does not clarify the focus ayah.
Repentance and divine mercy are relevant only as a broad remedy for disobedience.
A covenant rejects associating partners with God and commands obedience, supporting the positive alternative to idolatrous service.
The greeting to Moses and Aaron has no material connection.
The youths ask for mercy and right guidance, but not in relation to Satanic worship.
Calls Satan ungrateful toward his Lord, closely paralleling the focus ayah's description of his rebellion toward the Most Merciful.
The greeting to Elias is unrelated.
Divine forgiveness and mercy are too general to clarify Satan's rebellion.
Satan leads a person away from remembrance and then abandons him, directly explaining the danger Ibrahim names.
The greeting to Abraham alone does not develop the focus warning.
The standalone name the Most Merciful foregrounds the divine attribute invoked in the focus ayah.
Warns that Satan must not turn people away because he is a clear enemy, closely reinforcing Ibrahim's prohibition.
Prayer, almsgiving, and afterlife certainty do not specifically clarify the focus ayah.
A messenger's dissociation from those who disobey him parallels the later outcome of Ibrahim's rejected appeal.
Satan's domination makes people forget God and joins them to his party, directly illuminating what service to Satan entails.
The Most Merciful's harmonious creation only generally contrasts with Satan's rebellion.
Turning away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful results in a Satanic companion, a very close parallel to the focus wording.
Disobedience and transgression bring condemnation, but the verse lacks the focus's Satanic or worship link.
Warns Adam's children not to be tempted by Satan and identifies devils as allies of unbelievers, strongly supporting the warning.
States that invoking entities besides God is in fact invoking a rebellious Satan, directly explaining the focus's equation of idolatry with serving Satan.
Forbids following Satan's steps and explains their immoral direction, closely clarifying how service to Satan operates.
Ibrahim commands his people to worship God and fear Him, directly presenting the positive alternative in his own preaching.
Satan admits that he only called people and they answered him, directly explaining the voluntary allegiance warned against in the focus ayah.
Fear of disobeying the Lord is a direct moral contrast to Satan's rebellion, though without the worship context.
Prohibiting defense of traitors does not clarify the focus ayah.
God's kindness and mercy provide only a broad attribute parallel.
The speaker's refusal to worship what others worship is a concise contrast to the father's idolatry.
God's acceptance of repentance is a general counterpoint to persistent rebellion.
The Most Merciful's promise to His servants is only an attribute and servant-language parallel.
A servant receives mercy and divinely given knowledge, supporting the prophetic authority behind Ibrahim's instruction.
Without God's grace and mercy people would follow Satan; it closely links divine mercy to protection from Satanic following.
God's provision and knowledge do not address the focus warning.
A people resist a prophet's call to worship God alone because of ancestral worship, closely matching the father's idolatrous resistance.
Noah's faithful servitude is only a broad positive worship parallel.
Jacob's final question about whom his sons will worship contrasts inherited monotheistic commitment with the father's inherited idolatry.
Seeking refuge in the Most Merciful shows a protective use of the name but not the focus's Satanic relation.
The Forgiving and Merciful host believers, an attribute-level connection only.
Commands turning to God, fearing Him, praying, and avoiding polytheism, presenting the positive alternative to Satanic service.
Calls the Qur'an guidance and mercy for believers, supporting the merciful corrective purpose of Ibrahim's warning.
Punishment alone does not clarify Satanic worship, rebellion, or the paternal dialogue.
Forgiveness and mercy are too general to add to the focus ayah.
Worldly life's transience and the afterlife alternatives are too indirect.
Describes worship of powerless beings besides God, directly paralleling the idolatry Ibrahim condemns as Satanic service.
Declares that guidance belongs to God, grounding the divine alternative to Satan's path.
Rejects being commanded to worship other than God and calls such a demand ignorance, directly matching the focus's correction of idolatry.
Forbids following Satan's steps, directly clarifying the practical allegiance that Ibrahim prohibits.
Again forbids following Satan's steps and names him a clear enemy, a close general parallel to the focus warning.
Satan declares his intent to mislead and command people into corrupt acts, explaining the direction of service to him.
Satan's promises and false hopes explain the deceptive call behind the worship Ibrahim rejects.
Commands avoidance of practices described as Satan's defilement, supplying a concrete form of refusing his influence.
Obeying Satanic agents makes people associators, directly connecting obedience to Satan with idolatry.
Satan attributes his rebellion to his resolve to mislead humanity, closely explaining the adversary named in the focus ayah.
God denies Satan authority over His devoted servants, supplying the opposite allegiance to serving Satan.
Satan's authority is restricted to those who take him as an ally and associate partners with God, directly elucidating the focus warning.
Satan is permitted to summon and entice people, expanding the mechanism by which people answer his call.
God denies Satan power over His servants, sharply contrasting divine servitude with Satanic influence.
Iblis disobeys his Lord's command and people are warned not to take him and his offspring as allies, directly paralleling Satan's rebellion and forbidden allegiance.
Satan is identified as an enemy to Adam and his wife, reinforcing the warning not to align with him.
Satan whispers to Adam with a deceptive promise, showing the method of his leading astray.
Following every rebellious Satan is condemned, closely combining the focus ayah's themes of following and Satanic rebellion.
Whoever takes Satan as an ally is led astray and driven toward the Fire, directly clarifying the warning's consequence.
The Prophet seeks refuge from Satanic incitements, presenting the protective alternative to yielding to Satan.
Seeks refuge from Satan's presence, reinforcing active resistance to his influence.
Ibrahim asks his people what they worship, a closely related form of his corrective challenge to idolatry.
Ibrahim confronts the idols worshiped by his people and ancestors, directly extending his opposition to inherited false worship.
Ibrahim declares the objects they worship to be his enemies except the Lord of the worlds, supplying the positive allegiance behind the focus warning.
Ibrahim states that those worshiped besides God are idols and fabrications, directly reinforcing his rejection of his father's practice.
Abraham challenges worship of objects people carve, a concise and direct anti-idolatry parallel.
Those who avoid worshiping false powers and turn to God receive good news, clearly presenting the alternative to serving Satan.
Ibrahim declares himself free of what his father and people worship, directly paralleling his address to his father in the focus passage.
Ibrahim's exception for the One who created him identifies the true object of worship against the idols he rejects.
After guidance becomes clear, Satan makes turning back attractive and fills people with false hopes, explaining post-guidance apostasy.
Satan commands disbelief and then disavows his follower, illustrating the treacherous outcome of answering his call.
Commands refuge from the whisperer who withdraws, giving the direct spiritual countermeasure to Satanic prompting.
The whisperer casts suggestions into human hearts, explaining how Satanic influence is exercised.
Identifies the whisperer as from jinn and humankind, broadening the sources of Satanic-type temptation.
Satan frightens people through his allies, reinforcing the focus ayah's concern with Satanic allegiance.
Calls Satan an evil companion, a concise parallel to the danger of becoming connected to him.
Satan uses intoxicants and gambling to create enmity and turn people from God's remembrance and prayer, detailing a consequence of following him.
Depicts Satanic forces luring a person confused in the earth while companions call him back to guidance, closely contrasting Satanic and divine calls.
Names devils from humans and jinn as enemies of prophets who inspire deceptive speech, explaining organized resistance to prophetic correction.
Satan whispers to Adam and his wife in order to expose them, illustrating his deceptive prompting.
Satan deceives Adam and his wife by false assurances, further illustrating the character of the adversary Ibrahim names.
Satan makes opponents' deeds appear fair and then disavows them, a recurring pattern of Satanic deception and abandonment.
Satan causes Joseph's mention to be forgotten, providing a limited example of his obstructive influence.
Commands seeking God's refuge from the accursed Satan, the direct protective response to the danger in the focus ayah.
Denies Satan authority over believers who rely on their Lord, sharply contrasting trust in God with Satanic service.
Satan makes people's deeds appear fair and turns them from guidance, explaining how rebellion can be normalized.
Satan makes the queen and her people’s idolatry appear fair and bars them from the way, directly linking his influence to false worship.
Satan makes past peoples' deeds appear fair and bars them from the way, reinforcing his role in misguidance.
Commands people to take Satan as an enemy because he calls his party to the Blaze, directly supporting Ibrahim's prohibition against serving him.
Devils teach a harmful practice and are distinguished from the true source of knowledge, supporting the focus's rejection of Satanic allegiance.
Commands people to eat God's provision and not follow Satan's steps, a close imperative parallel to refusing Satanic service.
Satan can cause a believer to forget, showing a limited form of his influence but not worship or allegiance.
A man follows Satan and becomes among the erring, directly illustrating the ruinous result of following him.
Satan announces his intent to draw away nearly all of Adam's descendants, reinforcing his active opposition to human guidance.
Commands refuge in God when Satan incites, directly presenting resistance to the influence Ibrahim warns against.
Those mindful of God remember and regain clear sight when touched by Satanic prompting, giving the immediate corrective response to his influence.
Iblis's expectation is confirmed when people follow him except a believing group, directly depicting the divided allegiance at issue.
States that Satan led many people astray, immediately continuing the same discourse as the exact parallel in 36:60.
Satanic companions turn people from the path while they think themselves guided, closely explaining the danger of serving or following Satan.
